title: Grace (CCC 1996–2005)
hook: a free gift, God's own life shared with us

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Paraclete: the one called to your side, given with a breath. Your line was the breath of god. Did your breathing remind you? Today, what that breath brings with it. Day three hundred eight.

Someone pays for your coffee in the drive-through line, and drives off before you can thank them. What happens next varies. Some people want to pay it back, or pay it forward right away, or explain why they didn't really need it. A gift that can't be repaid takes the account out of our hands. Hold on to that moment. It sits close to the center of today's teaching. Catholics say the life of God in the soul is exactly that kind of gift.
screen: `SOMEONE PAYS FOR YOUR COFFEE.` → `PAY IT BACK? PAY IT FORWARD?` → `A GIFT YOU CAN'T REPAY.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Grace is the Latin gratia, and you can hear its cousin in gratis: free. The Greek is charis, a gift freely given. Paul says it in the Douay-Rheims: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." Second, what the gift is. The Catechism calls grace favor: the free and undeserved help God gives. But then it goes further. Grace is a share in God's own life. Not a thing God hands over from a distance. God giving himself. Third, two kinds. The Church speaks of sanctifying grace, a lasting gift that makes a person holy and friends with God, first given in baptism, and it's today's word. And it speaks of actual graces: God's help in particular moments, the nudge to call someone, the strength to hold your tongue. One is like the life of a tree. The other is like the rain on a given day. Fourth, earning. Since the Reformation, Catholics and Protestants have argued about grace and merit, sometimes bitterly. In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration saying together that people are accepted by God by grace alone, in faith in Christ, not because of any merit of their own. Catholics still speak of merit, and the Catechism explains that even merit is itself God's gift. A prayer of the Mass, drawing on Augustine, puts it this way: when God crowns our merits, he is crowning his own gifts.
screen: `GRATIA, GRATIS: FREE.` · `A SHARE IN GOD'S OWN LIFE.` · `THE TREE'S LIFE, THE DAY'S RAIN.` · `1999: BY GRACE ALONE, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `IT IS THE GIFT OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive one gift without earning it. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something good in your life that you did nothing to deserve. The family you were born into, a friend who stayed, your eyes, this morning's light. Don't explain it. Don't plan how to pay it back. Just receive it, the way you'd open your hands. If you pray, you can simply say thank you. The bell holds the time.
Sanctifying grace. The lasting gift of God's own life, first given in baptism, that makes a person holy and a friend of God. Free, not earned. Today's word.

Your line: free, not earned. Today, when someone does something kind for you, don't pay it back right away. Just say thank you, and let it be a gift. This week ran from the fall to the Word made flesh, Chalcedon, the Paschal mystery, the resurrection, the Spirit, and now grace. Day three hundred eight.
screen: `THIS WEEK: THE FALL · FLESH · CHALCEDON · PASCH · RISEN · SPIRIT · GRACE`

howItsDone: Catholics believe sanctifying grace is first given in baptism and is restored and strengthened through the sacraments, especially confession and the Eucharist; some also pray for the actual graces they need for a particular day or task.

fork.setup: a stranger pays for your coffee and drives off before you can say anything. which response fits what today's teaching says about grace?
options: chase them down to pay them back.
simply receive it and say thank you.
buy coffee for the next car immediately.
fork.reveal: simply receiving leaves the account in someone else's hands. Catholics say grace is exactly that kind of gift.

original.note: Greek: grace, favor, a gift freely given. Latin gratia.

trapdoor: what you thought: grace is being elegant, or saying grace before meals.
what it means: God's free gift of his own life, lasting in sanctifying grace and given moment by moment in actual graces.
what a scholar hears: charis and gratia; habitual and actual grace (CCC 2000); the 1999 Joint Declaration; Augustine on crowning his own gifts.
